headlines.summary: A bout of hard selling took hold of the market on Thursday, dragging the three major averages down to their worst session since April 2025.
headlines.article_text: Stock market today: Live updates Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Futures-options traders work on the floor at the New York Stock Exchange (NYSE) in New York City, US, Nov. 5, 2026. Jeenah Moon | Reuters Stock futures fell Thursday evening after a punishing sell-off in artificial intelligence stocks that sent the Nasdaq into correction territory. Traders also awaited a key payrolls report. S&P 500 futures lost 0.6%, while Nasdaq-100 futures slid 0.8%. Futures tied to the Dow Jones Industrial Average shed 291 points, or 0.6%. The moves follow a bout of heavy selling during Thursday's regular session that saw the three major averages post their worst one-day performances since April 2025. The Nasdaq Composite tanked 5.5%, closing more than 10% below its most recent high and landing in correction territory. The broad-market S&P 500 lost 4.4%, while the Dow fell more than 1,800 points, or 3.4%. While all 11 sectors of the S&P 500 closed with losses, shares of companies tied to the AI build-out suffered keenly. Democrats' big wins in the House and Senate, as well as key governorships in states like Texas, sparked traders' worries of a potential slowdown in data center construction. Micron Technology and Advanced Micro Devices plummeted 17% each, while neocloud CoreWeave slid 10%. Even the Magnificent Seven weren't spared, as Nvidia dropped 9%, turning negative for 2026, and the cohort of tech juggernauts shed more than $1 trillion in aggregate market cap. The three major averages are poised for losses on the week, with the Nasdaq down 4.4% and the S&P 500 off almost 3% in the period. The 30-stock Dow is the relative outperformer of the three, off just 0.5% week to date. The pullback creates a buying opportunity, Victoria Greene, CIO at G Squared Private Wealth told CNBC Thursday. "The AI trade, in my opinion, is not dead here," she said, adding, "it's a good discount." She's interested in memory stocks, citing how management teams throughout this earnings season have been talking about the capacity crunch. "Buying a volatile dip tends to be good as long as we're still in a non-recessionary period," she said. Another market catalyst awaits investors on Friday morning in the form of the October payrolls report. The Dow Jones consensus estimate is for 59,000 jobs added last month and for the unemployment rate to hold steady at 4.2%. Correction: Victoria Greene is the CIO of G Squared Private Wealth. An earlier version misspelled her name. 3 Min Ago Trump says Democrats are to blame for the stock market suffering President Donald Trump said, "The Stock Market suffered one of the Worst Days in History based on the results of the Election," in a post on Truth Social, late Thursday. The S&P 500, Nasdaq, and Russell 2000 all saw their worst sessions since April 2025, according to FactSet. The artificial intelligence-driven sell-off pushed the tech-heavy Nasdaq into correction territory. Democrats' big wins in the House and Senate ignited worries of a potential slowdown in data center construction. — Paulina Likos 24 Min Ago Asia-Pacific markets set to plunge after AI sell-off sinks Wall Street Asia-Pacific markets were set to open sharply lower Friday, tracking steep losses on Wall Street as a sell-off in technology stocks sent the Nasdaq Composite into correction territory. Futures for Japan's Nikkei 225 in Chicago were at 57,110 while in Osaka they were last at 57,400, compared with the index's previous close of 61,077.9. Futures for Hong Kong's Hang Seng index last traded at 24,494 compared with the index's last close of 24,796.98. Australia's S&P/ASX 200 was down over 1% in early trade. Concerns over the implications of a Democratic sweep in the U.S. midterm elections for the artificial intelligence sector have dented sentiment around AI plays, already under scrutiny over capex, profitability and debt. — Lee Ying Shan 12 Min Ago Job growth in October is expected to come in at 59,000, per Dow Jones The Bureau of Labor Statistics will release the October nonfarm payrolls Friday. Economists are expecting growth of 59,000 jobs, an increase from the 29,000 jobs produced in September, according to the Dow Jones consensus The unemployment rate is forecast to hold at 4.2%. The Federal Reserve sees the labor market as being on a solid footing, although uncertainty remains. The market is pricing in about a 70% chance of a 25-basis point interest rate hike at its Dec. 9 meeting, according to the CME FedWatch Tool . — Paulina Likos 13 Min Ago Megacap tech's 'Magnificent Seven' lost more than $1 trillion in market value The "Magnificent Seven" lost more than $1 trillion in aggregate market cap in Thursday's tech-led sell-off. IREN said the move, which could extend payment to February, is due to "a customer-requested change and supplier timing." On the company's earnings call, IREN co-CEO Daniel Roberts said Microsoft is the customer. "They made a request to reconfigure and upgrade some of the network infrastructure and the purpose of that was really to enable the 200 megawatts of capacity to service these latest-generation frontier models," Roberts said. Shares of IREN rose in extended trading, but that comes after a 55% drop over the past month. The company said revenue climbed 66% from the prior quarter to $228 million, beating the $221 million average analyst estimate, according to LSEG. AI Cloud revenue more than doubled to $200 million. IREN gets the rest of its revenue from bitcoin mining, which was its primary business before the company pivoted to AI. IREN's net loss narrowed to $263 million from $684 million the prior period. "Capital markets have become more selective in the last few weeks, and the questions have undoubtedly moved from how big the contract is to whether it can be delivered, financed, and run at a profit," Roberts said on the call. The $4 billion ARR target is fully contracted and funded, the company said. "There is a disconnect between what we're seeing in public market and what we're seeing at the customer level," Roberts told CNBC's Seema Mody. Still, Iren said it planed to shell out $15 billion in capital expenditures the rest of this fiscal year, including $9 billion in cash and committed financing, and $6 billion in "target" financing, which is "subject to market conditions." The neocloud said that prices for its compute continue to rise and that it expanded an existing contract with a leading frontier AI lab. It said it has contracts with Nvidia , Microsoft and 13 other customers. Roberts said that some data center construction in the coming year would be backed by Nvidia and Microsoft, but about a third would be to companies that are willing to offer large prepayments for the capacity. "We just had a customer agree to fund 90% of the GPU capex," Roberts said, referring to graphics processing units. IREN said that community opposition can be addressed by tapping local suppliers, using water efficiently and creating jobs. "I think whether it's Texas, whether it's Australia, whether it's Spain, everywhere, all we're seeing is people wanting to ensure that data centers pay their own way and do the right thing, and it it feels completely reasonable," Roberts said. IREN said it deliberately hadn't yet bought all of the GPUs it needs for next year to reduce risk. —CNBC's Isabel O'Brien contributed to this report. headlines.summary: Nasdaq’s slide into correction territory puts its history of recoveries in focus. Here's what history shows.
headlines.article_text: Nasdaq drops into correction territory — here’s what typically happens next Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu In this article .IXIC NDAQ Follow your favorite stocks CREATE FREE ACCOUNT Nasdaq 100 signage at the Nasdaq MarketSite in New York, US, on Thursday, Nov. 5, 2026. Michael Nagle | Bloomberg | Getty Images The Nasdaq Composite plunged into correction territory on Thursday. History shows more selling can follow in the near term, but a recovery eventually takes hold three months later. The tech-heavy index slid more than 5% on Thursday, closing more than 11% below its record reached last month. On Wall Street, any decline greater than 10% is a correction. A 20% pullback qualifies as a bear market. Across 10 previous correction episodes over the last decade, selloffs in 2025, 2022, 2020 and 2018 were followed by further rough selling over the next one month. But the Nasdaq was back to rally mode again after six months for all those occasions except one: 2022. Overall, the Nasdaq gained an average of 9.41% from the correction bottom over the following three months and 17.03% over six months. The January 2022 correction was the one that offered a harsher outcome. The Nasdaq lost another 18.3% over the next six months and was down 24.3% a year later. Nasdaq Composite Deena Zaidi and Nick Wells The catalyst for this correction was Democrats sweeping the House and Senate in Tuesday's midterm elections. The party also made significant gains in Texas, where Gina Hinojosa won the race for governor after campaigning on an immediate moratorium for data center development. Investors are now weighing whether tighter state-level restrictions could slow data center construction, putting pressure on companies tied to the artificial intelligence trade. Frank Cappelleri, founder of CappThesis, pointed to past midterm election cycles for guidance and found that points to more volatility in the near term as well. The chart analyst said the Nasdaq was higher 12 months after the election in all but one of 13 midterm cycles since 1974. "The caveat is that the path can be a volatile one," he said. Cappelleri pointed to 2018, when the Nasdaq rallied the day after Democrats won the House. A sharp December sell-off followed, but the index was ultimately about 15% higher a year after the election, he said. Chip stocks tumbled Thursday, with the iShares Semiconductor ETF (SOXX) falling 12% and for its worst day since the Covid-19 breakout of March 2020. — CNBC's Fred Imbert contributed to the report Choose CNBC as your preferred source on Google and never miss a moment from the most trusted name in business news.

headlines.article_text: Tesla, SpaceX stocks fall after 2026 midterms Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Key Points Elon Musk's Tesla and SpaceX lose over $420 billion in combined market cap in the two days after midterms. As Democrats control the House and Senate, and Texas flips blue, investors expect Musk and his companies to face probes and steeper regulatory hurdles to their AI and merger ambitions. Musk was the biggest backer of GOP candidates and causes in the midterms and most of those he backed were defeated by Dem opponents. In this article TSLA SPCX Follow your favorite stocks CREATE FREE ACCOUNT SpaceX CEO Elon Musk looks on as President Donald Trump speaks to the press after a meeting with technology executives about artificial intelligence at the White House in Washington, Sept. 29, 2026. Kent Nishimura | AFP | Getty Images SpaceX and Tesla shares declined by about 9% and 11%, respectively, on Thursday afternoon with investors concerned that Elon Musk could face new congressional probes — and his companies stricter regulation — following the U.S. midterm elections. The declines, which correlated with a broader tech sell-off , brought aggregate market cap losses for SpaceX and Tesla to over $420 billion since Tuesday's close. Musk's wealth, which had topped $1 trillion after SpaceX's initial public offering in June, is now down below $800 billion, having dropped about $90 billion in the past week, according to Forbes . He is still the richest man in the world. Musk was the biggest donor to GOP candidates and causes in the midterms, with his financial contributions exceeding $470 million , the Financial Times first reported. Despite his bolstering the GOP war chest, most of the candidates Musk backed lost their races . Democrats won control of both the House and Senate. And in Texas, where both Tesla and SpaceX are headquartered, Democrats Sen.-elect James Talarico and Gov.-elect Gina Hinojosa beat longtime Musk allies, state Attorney General Ken Paxton and Gov. Greg Abbott. Deutsche Bank analysts wrote in a note out on Wednesday, "While policy is naturally hard to predict, we could envision SpaceX facing some incremental headwinds in this type of backdrop." Gov.-elect Hinojosa "made data centers a major campaign issue," the analysts noted, calling for "a moratorium on new approvals until the legislature passes stronger protections on water use, electricity costs, local control, and incentives," and criticizing tax breaks for large facilities. Tesla and SpaceX are both building out AI infrastructure in Texas, and are planning to build Terafab, a massive facility, which will include a data center and sprawling semiconductor factory, in Grimes County, Texas. SpaceX also plans to build out a "supercomputer" at its Starbase, Texas, launch facility and company town, according to company job listings . Deutsche Bank analysts also wrote that SpaceX's Texas compute capacity could now be at risk of delays. Capital expenditures by the company may need to increase to meet the requirements of tighter, anticipated regulations around data center buildout, the analysts wrote. Musk and SpaceX have been instructed to preserve records concerning restrictions imposed on a military version of the Starlink satellite internet service in Ukraine, CNN first reported , citing an aide to a Democratic senator. The restrictions hampered the country's ability to defend against attacks by Russia. Additionally, regulatory scrutiny could block chances for Musk to merge SpaceX and Tesla, an idea he has promoted, while acknowledging shareholders' approval would be required first. SpaceX and Tesla had lost about $456 billion in market cap by the close of business on Thursday. The lawmakers invited Huang to appear for an in-person joint briefing on Nov. 18, the day after Nvidia is scheduled to report its third-quarter earnings. Graeme Sloan | Bloomberg | Getty Images Three House Republican committee leaders asked Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang to sit for a closed-door briefing on his relationship with a tech executive reportedly identified as a Chinese intelligence asset. "Recent reports raise significant national security concerns regarding the PRC's access to sensitive U.S. technology and information," the GOP lawmakers wrote in a letter to Huang unveiled Thursday, using the acronym for the People's Republic of China. They are seeking information on Huang's interactions with Megaspeed executive Alice Huang, as well as Nvidia's "security protocols against foreign adversary espionage," they wrote in the brief message, which is dated Wednesday. The letter does not specify which reports it is referring to. But The New York Times reported last week that U.S. intelligence found Alice Huang, a Chinese citizen determined to be funneling information to Beijing, had "developed a close relationship" with Jensen Huang. Read more CNBC politics and policy coverage Midterm elections 2026 live updates: Economy, inflation and voter concerns 5 midterm election takeaways: Tech billionaires suffer as Democrats drub Republicans Elon Musk’s record election bet backfired. The backlash may reach beyond one billionaire Analysis: The Democrats have one chance to extract concessions from Trump. Markets will hate it President Donald Trump , who himself has forged close ties with Jensen Huang as he champions the U.S. artificial intelligence industry, was briefed about a year ago on those intelligence findings, the Times reported. Trump "chose not to do anything with the information," according to the newspaper, which cited interviews with people briefed on the surveillance and other sources. The letter to Huang was signed by House Foreign Affairs Committee Chairman Brian Mast, R-Fla., Select Committee on China Chairman John Moolenaar, R-Mich., and House Permanent Select Committee on Intelligence Chairman Rick Crawford, R-Ark. Nvidia did not directly respond when asked by CNBC to comment on the letter and confirm whether Huang would attend the lawmakers' proposed briefing. Nvidia instead provided a statement that largely mirrored the one it previously sent the Times, in which a spokesperson suggested Jensen Huang's interactions with Alice Huang were no different from his meetings with other executive clients. "Our regional cloud customers receive ordinary business information — not sensitive NVIDIA trade secrets—and zero information relevant to national security," the spokesperson said in the statement. "Meetings with customers are part of a CEO's job; Jensen talks with thousands of customer executives every year," the spokesperson said. "We're confident that if the U.S. government believes that any person is a threat to American industry, it would let us know." A spokeswoman for Mast did not immediately respond to CNBC's request for additional information. Megaspeed did not immediately respond to an email seeking comment. The lawmakers invited the Nvidia CEO to appear for an in-person joint briefing on Nov. 18. Nvidia is scheduled to report its third-quarter earnings on Nov. 17. "China's access to that sensitive U.S. tech is core to the investigative work of our three committees this Congress," the committee leaders wrote. "It is vital that Congress determines the extent to which U.S. national security has been placed at risk."
